parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alausa, from Gaulish *alausa. Doublet of alose.

parole.significato: A member of the Arverns or Arverni, the ancient Gaulish (Celtic) tribe which inhabited what is now the Auvergne region…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Arvernus, borrowed from Gaulish.

parole.significato: Order of battle; disposition or arrangement of troops or of a naval force, ready for action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (“military exercises”), from Latin battuō (“to strike, beat”), from Gaulish. Doublet of battle.

parole.significato: A coarse kind of thick woollen cloak, worn by the poor in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin birrus (“a kind of cloak”), from Gaulish *birros, from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”).

parole.significato: Shapeless trousers of wool or skin tied at the waist and ankles by cords, worn chiefly by the ancient Gauls.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracae, plural of braca, from Gaulish *brāca, of Celtic origin, cognate with Proto-Germanic *brōks; akin to Old High German bruoh (“a pair of breeches”) and to Dutch broek (“a pair of trousers”).

parole.significato: A layer of cells between the xylem and the phloem that is responsible for the secondary growth of roots and stems.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cambium (“a change”), from Gaulish. Doublet of change.

parole.significato: A unit of itinerary distance varying with country, in Britain commonly about three statute miles (or five kilometres).…
parole.testo: From Middle English lege (“league”), from Late Latin leuca, leuga (“the Gaulish mile”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *lougā (compare Middle Breton leau, lew, Breton lev / leo (“league”)). Doublet of legua.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the region of Poitou in France.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French poitevin, ultimately from Late Latin pictāvīnus, from Pictāvus (“Poitou”), of Gaulish origin. See Poitiers and Poitou.

parole.significato: A cloak, worn in ancient times by the Gauls, early Germans, and Roman soldiers, made of a rectangular piece of (usually…
parole.testo: From Latin sagum, perhaps of Gaulish origin.

parole.significato: The winged indehiscent fruit of trees such as the ash, elm or maple.
parole.testo: From Latin samara (“elm seed”), from a Gaulish term derived from Proto-Celtic *samos (“summer”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Venice or surrounding province, Veneto region, northeastern Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Venetianus (“Venetic; Venetian”), from Venetia (“lands of the Veneti; Venice, Veneto; Armorica”) + -anus (“-ian”), from Veneti + -ia. parole.significato: A magistrate in ancient Gaul who held the highest office in many Gallic cities, especially among the Aedui.
parole.testo: From Latin vergobretus (“chief magistrate amongst the Aedui”), from Gaulish uercobretos.
